title: not statues
hook: not statues — people with terrible flaws who kept going
tomorrow: the rich kid who gave his clothes back

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mary: a young woman, a question, and a yes. Your line was: let it be. And that's a week. Grace, the sign of the cross, the Gospel, the sign of peace, the Eucharist, Mary. Day seven.

Walk into an old Catholic church and you'll see them everywhere. Plaster figures in niches. Faces in stained glass. A man holding keys, a woman holding a wheel, a guy with a lamb. They look calm and a little unreal, like people who never had a bad day in their lives. That's the picture most people carry of a saint: someone born good, floating above it all. Catholics would tell you that picture is almost exactly wrong. The man holding the keys once swore three times that he'd never met his best friend. Today's word: not statues, people.
screen: `FACES IN STAINED GLASS.` → `THEY LOOK UNREAL.` → `NOT STATUES. PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Saint comes from the Latin sanctus, holy. In the New Testament, Paul writes letters to the saints in Rome and Corinth, and he means ordinary believers, people with jobs and arguments and debts. Later, the word came to mean especially the people the Church believes are now with God in heaven, and holds up as examples. So take the man with the keys. That's Peter. On the night Jesus was arrested, Peter was asked three times whether he knew him, and three times he said no. Then a rooster crowed, and the Gospels say he went out and wept bitterly. That's the first leader of the apostles, the one Catholics count as the first pope. Or take Augustine, one of the greatest thinkers the Church ever had. In his Confessions he admits that as a young man he prayed, more or less, make me pure, but not yet. Or Paul himself, who spent his early years hunting down Christians. The saints aren't people who never fell. They're people who fell and kept getting up. Here's the part Catholics love. They believe in what the old creed calls the communion of saints: that the living and the dead who belong to Christ are one family, and the family can still pray for each other. So a Catholic might ask a saint to pray for them the way you'd ask a grandmother. The statues are something like family photos on the wall. Nobody prays to the plaster. It's a reminder of who else is in the room. Other Christians see it differently: many Protestants honor the saints as examples and don't ask them for prayers. But the stories are the same stories. Flawed people, still going.
screen: `SANCTUS — HOLY.` · `PETER SAID NO THREE TIMES.` · `AUGUSTINE: BUT NOT YET.` · `THE COMMUNION OF SAINTS.` · then, large: `FLAWED PEOPLE, STILL GOING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice for the end of week one. Three breaths, with the bell. Think of one person, alive or gone, who failed at something and kept going, and who you're glad you knew. On the first breath, picture their face. On the second, remember what they got wrong. On the third, remember that they kept going. If you pray, you can thank God for them.
The saints. Holy ones: people who fell and got up, and who Catholics believe are still one family with the living. Seventh word.
Your line: the company you're in. Today, when you mess something up, remember that the saints did too, and kept going. Day seven. One week.

screen: `DAY 7 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE RICH KID WHO GAVE HIS CLOTHES BACK.`

howItsDone: Catholics celebrate saints' feast days through the year and on All Saints' Day, November 1; many are named for a saint and ask the saints, especially their patron saint, to pray for them.

Peter denied Jesus three times. Paul hunted Christians. they fell and got up.

fork.setup: you're Peter, standing by a fire the night Jesus is arrested. a servant girl asks if you know him. what does Peter do?
options: says yes, and is arrested too.
fork.reveal: three times he says he doesn't know him. then the rooster crows, and he weeps. Catholics count him the first pope.

original.note: Greek: holy, set apart. Paul's word for all believers; Latin sanctus.

trapdoor: what you thought: perfect people carved in plaster.
what it means: flawed people who kept going, and who Catholics believe are still one family with the living.
what a scholar hears: hagioi, Paul's name for every believer; later, formal canonization; the communion of saints, sanctorum communio, from the Apostles' Creed.

notes: Augustine's prayer (Confessions 8.7.17, 'give me chastity and continence, but not yet') is paraphrased as 'make me pure, but not yet'. Confirm the paraphrase is acceptable.
Saint iconography: Peter with keys, Catherine of Alexandria with a wheel, Agnes or John the Baptist with a lamb; the hook names objects only. Confirm.
Peter as first pope: stated as Catholic belief ('the one Catholics count as the first pope'). Confirm.
